summary:
Nostromo-I is a web app that allowes users to explore weather trends anywhere in the world. A user picks a location and a variable, such as air temperature, rainfall, soil moisture or aerosol optical depth, or asks a question in natural language.

The app pulls monthly data from NASA GLDAS, GPM IMERG and MERRA-2 through Giovanni and Earthdata. It then answers the four questions in the challenge: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant.

The system has a deterministic base. We remove the seasonal cycle, then run two tests that adjust for autocorrelation (Hamed-Rao Mann-Kendall with Sen's slope, and a linear regression using an effective sample size). We report rates per decade with 95% confidence intervals and correct for testing many variables at once (Benjamini-Hochberg). For trends that are not yet significant, we estimate how many more years of data would be needed. Our code reproduces NASA GISTEMP's published global warming rates of 0.18 and 0.17 °C per decade. An optional AI assistant turns questions into analyses and writes plain-language verdicts, but it never produces numbers.

This matters because loose claims like "it's getting hotter here" become measurable evidence anyone can check.
details:
Description and methodology

Nostromo-I is a web application for detecting and quantifying weather trends in Earth observation and model data. For a user-specified location, period and set of variables, it addresses four questions: which variables are changing, where, at what rate, and whether the change is statistically significant. Analyses can be specified through a structured form or as a natural-language question, which is converted into a form draft that the user reviews before submission.

The analysis proceeds in four stages.

  1. Data acquisition. Monthly point time series are retrieved from GLDAS Noah (land surface model), GPM IMERG (satellite-derived precipitation) and MERRA-2 (atmospheric reanalysis) via the NASA Giovanni time-series service and Earthdata. Every request is subject to a timeout, and raw responses are cached so that analyses can be reproduced.
    • a non-parametric approach: the Mann-Kendall test with the Hamed-Rao variance correction for autocorrelation, together with the Theil-Sen slope estimator;
    • a parametric approach: ordinary least squares regression with the standard error recomputed from an effective sample size, n_eff = n(1 − r₁)/(1 + r₁), where r₁ is the lag-1 autocorrelation of the residuals.
  2. Multiple-comparison control. When several variables are evaluated jointly, the false discovery rate is controlled with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. For trends that are not significant, the application estimates the additional record length required for significance, given the observed slope and residual variance.

Results are presented on an interactive three-dimensional globe, together with anomaly time series, confidence-interval displays and a four-level summary of the evidence: strong evidence, mixed signals, no clear trend yet and record too short. A regional mode repeats the per-cell analysis over a circle of radius 1.25° (about 140 km) around the point of interest, with false discovery rate control applied across cells. This shows whether a point trend reflects a broader spatial pattern. The application also supports side-by-side comparison of two locations and keeps a public archive of completed analyses.

Validation

  • Simulation study. Unit tests on synthetic series with a known slope, Gaussian noise, seasonality and AR(1) persistence check the empirical Type I error rate, statistical power and confidence-interval coverage of both procedures.
  • Reproduction of published estimates. Applied to the NASA GISTEMP v4 global land-ocean temperature anomaly, the implementation yields 0.179 °C per decade for 1970–2010 (95% CI: 0.158–0.199), compared with a published value of 0.18 (Hansen et al., 2025). For January 1979 to April 2016 it yields 0.175 °C per decade (95% CI: 0.150–0.200), compared with a published 0.17 (Simmons et al., 2016).

Benefits and intended impact

The project aims to make statistically sound trend analysis accessible to users without specialized training, including students, educators, journalists and local decision-makers. Its three demonstration studies, each testing a hypothesis stated in advance from the published literature, illustrate the intended use.

  • Agriculture and agronomy: trends in soil moisture, precipitation, evapotranspiration and near-surface air temperature, relevant to crop water demand, irrigation planning and growing conditions.
  • Hydrology and water resources management: changes in precipitation, surface runoff, evaporation and root-zone soil moisture, particularly in water-stressed regions such as northern Mexico.
  • Climate science: local and regional detection of temperature, humidity and radiation trends, with explicit treatment of autocorrelation and multiple testing.
  • Public health and air quality: long-term changes in aerosol optical depth and heat exposure.
  • Ecology and environmental science: shifts in canopy water storage, transpiration and land-surface temperature that affect ecosystems.
  • Renewable energy: trends in incoming shortwave radiation and near-surface wind speed, relevant to solar and wind resource assessment.
  • Urban and regional planning, and disaster risk reduction: evidence of warming, drying or changes in precipitation to inform adaptation planning.
  • Education and science communication: a transparent, reproducible example of how environmental trends are tested, suited to teaching and to journalism.

Reporting null and contradictory results alongside confirmatory ones is intentional. The application also presents the estimated time to significance and the agreement between tests, so that users understand why short or noisy records may not yet support a firm conclusion.

Tools and technologies

  • Data sources: NASA Earthdata, Giovanni time-series API, GLDAS Noah, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2, GISTEMP v4 (validation).
  • Scientific computing (Python 3.12): earthaccess, xarray, netCDF4, pandas, numpy, scipy, statsmodels, pymannkendall; tested with pytest.
  • Backend: FastAPI and SQLModel, with SQLite for local development and PostgreSQL (Neon) in production, deployed on Render.
  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, react-globe.gl/Three.js, Plotly.js and D3 color scales; tested with Vitest and Playwright.
  • Language model (optional): Anthropic Claude converts natural-language questions into form drafts and writes plain-language summaries of results. Every number in a generated summary is checked against the computed results, with a deterministic template as the fallback. The language model never produces, alters or estimates numbers, and the application is fully functional without it.
  • Hardware: standard personal computers; no specialized hardware was required.

Current state

  • Separation of computation and interpretation. The language model only translates and explains, and all reported numbers come from tested statistical code. This prevents fabricated figures in AI-assisted scientific communication.
  • Dual testing with explicit disagreement reporting. Presenting both test results, and flagging when they disagree, conveys how robust a finding is better than a single p-value does.
  • Time to significance. For trends that are not significant, the estimated additional record length reframes a null result as a statement about the available data rather than about the absence of change.
  • Integrated point and regional analysis, which places a local trend in its spatial context within the same interface.

Design considerations

  • Statistical rigor. Seasonality, serial correlation and multiple testing each inflate false-positive rates if left unaddressed, and the methodology corrects for each explicitly. The analysis is limited to linear trends, and the application states this.
  • Reproducibility. Cached raw responses, a versioned method and committed precomputed results allow every reported figure to be regenerated.
  • Transparency. Units, data source, record length and both p-values accompany every result.
  • Acknowledged limitations. Single grid cells do not resolve sub-grid urban effects, and model and reanalysis products are not equivalent to station observations. These caveats are stated in the application.
  • Operational robustness. Because of the variable availability of NASA services during the event, the demonstration studies are precomputed so that presentation does not depend on live data retrieval.
  • Security and accessibility. Credentials are kept in environment variables and are never committed. A glossary and a guided introduction support first-time users.
